detail: supported
An adaptation of the WYSIWYG (What You See Is What You Get) concept to volumetric exploration, implementing a high-level semantic representation with drawing tools [S4, unofficial].

The claim is a direct translation of the sentence found in Source [S4]: 'Guo, Mao e Yuan (2011) adaptaram o conceito WYSIWYG (do inglês, What You See is What You Get) à exploração volumétrica, implementando uma representação de alto nível semântico que disponibiliza ferramentas de desenho ao usuário.' This translates to: 'Guo, Mao, and Yuan (2011) adapted the WYSIWYG concept to volumetric exploration, implementing a high-level semantic representation that provides drawing tools to the user.' All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported
A transfer function design workflow where users select Sources of Interest (SOIs) directly in visualization space (2D cross-sections or 3D DVR) instead of indirect TF widgets [S3, unofficial].

The claim states that the workflow involves users selecting Sources of Interest (SOIs) directly in visualization space (2D cross-sections or 3D DVR) instead of indirect TF widgets. Source [S3] explicitly confirms this in Section 5.2, stating: 'Our CBR-TF approach required a user to simply draw a line in 2D cross-sectional views... or a point in 3D DVRs... to select SOIs.' It further emphasizes that this is an 'image-centric interaction to directly select SOIs in a visualization space, not in an indirect TF widget space.' Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
The system retrieves matching SOIs via a two-stage Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) method [S3, unofficial].

The claim states that the system retrieves matching SOIs via a two-stage Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) method. The evidence in Source [S3] explicitly states: 'System retrieves matching SOIs via the two-stage CBR method.' Additionally, the passages mention that 'our two-stage method performed better in precision' and refer to the approach as 'CBR-TF'. Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
Right-handed horizontal touch-swipe changes painting transparency and brush radius, which scales by zoom level [S5, unofficial].

The claim states that 'Right-handed horizontal touch-swipe changes painting transparency and brush radius, which scales by zoom level'. Source [S5] explicitly states: 'Right-handed horizontal touch-swipe changes the painting transparency and the brush radius. The brush radius is scaled by the zoom level.' All facts in the claim are directly supported by the text in Source [S5].
supported
A VR painting interface using off-the-shelf controllers (HTC Vive) with specific gestures for transparency, radius, and color selection [S5, unofficial].

The claim states that the VR painting interface uses off-the-shelf controllers (HTC Vive) with specific gestures for transparency, radius, and color selection. The evidence in Source [S5] explicitly confirms: 1) The use of 'off-the-shelf VR controllers such as HTC Vive controllers'; 2) 'Right-handed horizontal touch-swipe changes the painting transparency and the brush radius'; and 3) A 'novel 3D color picking interface' where the user moves the controller inside an RGB-color cube to change the brush color. All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported

Tory et al. [89] introduced a parallel coordinates style interface to provide an overview of rendering options and transfer function settings, facilitating parameter exploration and history backtracking [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that Tory et al. [89] introduced a parallel coordinates style interface for overviewing rendering options and transfer function settings, facilitating parameter exploration and history backtracking. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Tory et al. [89] propose a parallel coordinates style interface that provides an overview of rendering options and transfer function settings. The user can easily explore different parameters and backtrack the visualization history using the proposed interface.' All facts in the claim are present and consistent with the evidence.
supported
The user moves the controller inside the RGB-color cube to change brush color, and can rotate/translate the cube [S5, unofficial].

The claim states that the user moves the controller inside the RGB-color cube to change brush color and can rotate/translate the cube. Source [S5] explicitly states: 'Our color picker displays a RGB-color cube, and the user can move the controller inside the cube to change the brush color. The user can also rotate or translate the cube.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
False-negative SOIs (missing structures) require manual addition, but starting from scratch is avoided [S3, unofficial].

The claim states that false-negative SOIs require manual addition but starting from scratch is avoided. The evidence in Source [S3] explicitly states: 'Such manual TF optimization can be more challenging in missing structures (i.e., false-negative). However, our CBR-TF approach is still effective because the user does not need to start the TF design from scratch, and it is easier to add new SOIs to the TF that already contains other SOIs.' This confirms both parts of the claim: the need for manual handling of false negatives (adding new SOIs) and the avoidance of starting from scratch.
supported

The user manually eliminates TF components for false-positive SOIs if retrieval errors occur [S3, unofficial].

The claim states that users manually eliminate TF components for false-positive SOIs if retrieval errors occur. The evidence in Source [S3] explicitly states: 'In the cases when the false-positive from our SOI retrieval occurs, we note that the user needs to manually eliminate the TF component of the falsepositive SOI.' This directly supports the claim.

The claim states that TFs are constructed by combining individual tent-shape components, each representing a retrieved SOI. The evidence in Source [S3] explicitly states: 'In our CBR-TF approach, TFs were comprised of individual tent-shape components to represent each SOI.' This directly supports the claim.

Rule extension draws a connection from a semantic-property widget to an expression-tree widget to include the semantic property as an additional operand [S2].

The claim states that 'Rule extension draws a connection from a semantic-property widget to an expression-tree widget to include the semantic property as an additional operand.' This is explicitly confirmed in the Source [S2] notes under 'Rule Extension' and in the final passage of Source [S2], which states: 'Drawing a connection from a semantic-property widget to an expression-tree widget allows users to extend the rule represented by the expression tree. The semantic property is included as an additional operand in the rule.'

A novel 3D color picking interface allows one-handed color selection using an RGB-color cube [S5, unofficial].

The claim states that a novel 3D color picking interface allows one-handed color selection using an RGB-color cube. The evidence in Source [S5] explicitly mentions: 'we implemented a novel 3D color picking interface that allows user to select brush-color using a left-handed controller while drawing' and 'Our color picker displays a RGB-color cube, and the user can move the controller inside the cube to change the brush color.' This confirms all aspects of the claim.
